conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I started vomiting bile last night—no blood—and the pain got worse. It feels just like my past bowel blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of sclerosing mesenteritis and recurrent obstructions. Did you try anything at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took extra Phenergan and morphine, but it didn’t help. I still passed gas, though, so I wasn’t completely blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good you’re still passing gas. We did a CT scan and a plain X-ray. The CT shows your duodenum is more dilated than before, suggesting a partial blockage, but contrast is moving through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a full blockage? But it feels just like the last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a partial or transient obstruction, related to your mesenteritis. We’ll keep you NPO for now, give IV fluids, and vent your stomach through the G-tube to relieve pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my warfarin? My INR was 5.0 in the ER—that’s high, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s elevated. We’re holding your warfarin for now in case we need any procedures. We’ll restart it when you’re more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show mild dehydration and low potassium. We’re correcting that with IV fluids and supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been feeling a bit weak. Is the fatty liver on the CT related to my hepatitis C?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. But your liver enzymes are stable, and ammonia is normal, so it’s not causing your current symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better—bowel sounds are returning. We’re going to start clear liquids slowly and cap your G-tube to see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go back on my regular meds soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting your metoclopramide and misoprostol to help gut motility. Aciphex isn’t available here, so we’re using famotidine for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been tolerating liquids well. We’re advancing to a soft diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We scheduled a small bowel follow-through to check your motility. It’s a test where you drink contrast, and we watch it move through your intestines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it make me nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give anti-nausea meds beforehand. It’s important to see if your bowels are moving properly despite the structural changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the SBFT showed normal motility. The contrast reached the colon in 50 minutes, which is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I keep getting these blockage-like episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your anatomy is altered from mesenteritis—dilated loops, tethering—but the function is okay. It’s likely transient partial obstructions due to inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re going to try restarting your home medications fully, including Lyrica and Lamictal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired and a bit confused since yesterday. Could that be from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We checked your liver and ammonia—both normal. We think the altered mental status is from restarting Lyrica and Lamictal at full dose too quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to hold Lyrica for now and reduce Lamictal to 25mg. We’ll increase slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been anxious and having trouble sleeping too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue trazodone and lorazepam as needed. Social work will also check in to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting TPN today. Nutrition feels it’s needed because you’re not meeting your needs by mouth, especially after the setback.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was hoping to avoid TPN. I’ve had complications before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But with your malnutrition and risk of further obstruction, TPN will help you heal and maintain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable. We’re continuing TPN and your oral diet. We’ll keep monitoring your G-tube output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m having more pain again, and I vomited. My G-tube just drained over 1300cc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry. We’re going back to NPO and IV fluids. A new X-ray shows ileus, not a full obstruction. It should resolve with rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this going to keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s frustrating, I know. Your underlying condition makes you prone to these episodes. We’re adjusting your pain plan to avoid heavy IV opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ileus is improving. We’re restarting oral meds and will try clears again soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another X-ray shows diffuse bowel distention—likely ileus again. We’ll hold oral intake for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so tired of being stuck in bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s hard. But your body needs time. We’re continuing TPN and will try liquids again when you stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The distention is improving. We’re seeing better motility. We’ll try small sips of water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. We’re advancing diet slowly. We’ve restarted warfarin at your home dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my Lyrica and Lamictal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted Lyrica at a lower dose—75mg twice daily—and increased Lamictal to 50mg. We’ll keep titrating up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: X-ray shows moderate fecal loading but no obstruction. We’re adding bisacodyl to help with bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated. Should I take more senna?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching to bisacodyl for now. We’ll adjust as needed. Docusate will stay for softening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable. We’re continuing TPN at home. Your gastroenterologist will follow up on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home on TPN. What if I have another flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you clear instructions. If vomiting or severe pain returns, come back. Otherwise, keep your GI follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge tomorrow. You’re on oral pain meds—morphine SR and liquid as needed—and tizanidine for muscle spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still need the G-tube venting at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if you feel bloated or nauseous. Otherwise, keep it capped. Use Phenergan as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dry eyes from Sjogren’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending artificial tears. Pilocarpine isn’t available here, but your regular doctor can restart it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re being discharged today. Your vitals are stable, and you’re managing symptoms well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It’s been a long stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had a setback, but you’ve recovered. Continue TPN, all meds, and follow up with your PCP and GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I just hope I can avoid another hospitalization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all do. But now you know the signs. Don’t hesitate to reach out if things worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything you’ve done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard too. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.
